project.topic: What if it rained nonstop everywhere on Earth for a year?
project.title: What If It Rained Nonstop Everywhere for a Year?
project.audience: Curious global general audiences age 13+, no science background
project.core_question: If gentle rain fell everywhere on Earth without a break for a whole year, which places would win, which would lose, and could the rain keep itself going?
project.viewer_takeaway: Rain is recycled water lifted by sunlight, so nonstop rain everywhere would be a gentle drizzle of about a meter a year: deserts could green, rainforests would get less, farms and solar panels would suffer, and the clouds would block the very sunlight that powers the rain.

scientific_model.baseline_reality: Today rain is patchy in space and time: about two thirds of Earth is under cloud at any moment, deserts such as the central Sahara get only millimetres to a few centimetres a year, and rainforests get two to ten metres. The atmosphere holds only about 12,900 km³ of water, enough for 2.5 cm of rain over the whole globe, so rain must be constantly recycled by evaporation, which uses about a quarter of the sunlight reaching Earth.
scientific_model.counterfactual_change: From one day on and for one year, every place on Earth is under a continuous rain-bearing cloud deck and gentle rain falls without a break. Physics is unchanged: the total amount of rain is still limited by the energy available to evaporate water, so the global yearly total stays about the same (about a metre) but is spread evenly in space and time. At the poles and high mountains it falls as snow.
assumptions: The water cycle keeps its present strength at first: evaporation uses about 25% of incoming sunlight (NASA), which corresponds to roughly 1.1 m of water per year averaged over the globe; spread evenly this is about 3 mm a day, or about 0.12 mm an hour.
Rain falls everywhere at the same gentle rate; where temperatures are below freezing it falls as snow (Antarctica, Greenland, high mountains).
Geography, oceans and the composition of the air are unchanged; the film follows first-year consequences and does not claim a final climate state.
How such a planet-wide cloud deck could arise is not addressed; it is the thought experiment.
causal_chain: The atmosphere holds only about 2.5 cm of rain, so year-long rain must be recycled by evaporation from the oceans and land.
Evaporation is powered by sunlight and uses about a quarter of it, which limits global rainfall to roughly a metre a year.
Spread evenly, every place gets about 3 mm a day: a gentle drizzle rather than a flood.
Deserts such as the Sahara get dozens of times their usual rain and could begin to green, as the Sahara did during the African Humid Period about 11,000–5,000 years ago.
Rainforests, which normally get 2–10 m a year, would get less rain than now.
Farms lose dry days for ripening and harvest, so grain can mould or sprout; solar panels produce less under constant cloud.
A cloud deck everywhere reflects more sunlight, so less energy reaches the surface to evaporate water and the rain would likely weaken over time.
uncertainties: Whether an unbroken global cloud deck could exist at all is not established; the film treats it as a premise.

The net effect of total cloud cover on temperature depends on cloud height and thickness (clouds reflect sunlight but also trap heat at night); the direction of the rain weakening is plausible but its size is not quantified.
How fast desert vegetation would respond in a single year is uncertain; the film says the Sahara could start to green, not that it would become a savanna.
Regional responses (soils, rivers, ecosystems) would vary widely and are shown only as examples.

claims.statement: The atmosphere holds about 12,900 km³ of water at any one time; if it all fell at once it would cover the globe only about 2.5 cm deep.
claims.reasoning: USGS Water Science School, The Atmosphere and the Water Cycle.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Say "two and a half centimeters"; the air column is labelled schematic and not to scale.

claims.statement: About 67 percent of Earth's surface is typically covered by clouds.
claims.reasoning: NASA Earth Observatory (Cloudy Earth), from about a decade of MODIS satellite data.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Show as an approximate chip on the TODAY view.

claims.statement: Rainfall is very unevenly spread: much of the Sahara gets almost no rain; Egypt, for example, received only 18 mm in all of 2017, against 3,240 mm in Colombia.
claims.reasoning: USGS Water Science School, Precipitation and the Water Cycle.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Use "bone dry" and "dozens of times" rather than a single exact multiplier.

claims.statement: Spread evenly, Earth's yearly rain would be roughly 1.1 m everywhere, about 3 mm a day or about 0.12 mm an hour, a gentle drizzle.
claims.reasoning: NASA: about 25% of incoming solar energy (340 W/m² average) leaves the surface through evaporation, about 85 W/m²; divided by the latent heat of vaporisation (2.45 MJ/kg) this is about 1,100 kg/m² of water a year; 1.1 m / 365 ≈ 3 mm per day.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Narrate "about a meter" and "about three millimeters a day"; label as a global average.

claims.statement: Rain is powered by sunlight: evaporation takes about a quarter of incoming solar energy, and the latent heat is released when the vapour condenses back into rain.
claims.reasoning: NASA Earth Observatory, Climate and Earth's Energy Budget.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Show vapour as labelled illustrative rising specks.

claims.statement: Roughly 11,000 to 5,000 years ago, during the African Humid Period, the Sahara was much wetter and greener, with vegetation, wetlands and perhaps large lakes.
claims.reasoning: NASA Earth Observatory, Water for a Desert Lake in Algeria.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Narrate "some eight thousand years ago" (inside that period); show the period range on screen.

claims.statement: With about a metre of rain in a year, much of the Sahara could begin to green, starting with grasses and annual plants in hollows.
claims.reasoning: Desert annuals and grasses germinate quickly after rain; sustained rain far above today's totals favours vegetation, as during the African Humid Period.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Say "could turn green"; label the greening time-lapse illustrative and partial.

claims.statement: Rainforests typically receive 2,000 to 10,000 mm of rain a year, so an even metre would mean less rain for them.
claims.reasoning: The NASA rainforest biome page gives 2,000–10,000 mm a year; an even 1.1 m is less than every value in that range.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Narrate "two meters or more"; the gauge comparison is a schematic.

claims.statement: Excessive rain and delayed harvest give mould more time to grow on grain, raise mycotoxins and can make grain sprout before harvest.
claims.reasoning: Ohio State University Extension, Wet Weather, Potential Wheat Harvest Delays, and Grain Quality (2023).
claims.presentation_guardrail: Say "can rot"; show soaked wheat, not spoiled food close-ups.

claims.statement: Clouds hamper solar panels' ability to produce electricity.
claims.reasoning: U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Use an illustrative gauge without a percentage.

claims.statement: A cloud deck covering the whole planet would reflect more sunlight, leaving less energy at the surface to evaporate water, so the rain would likely weaken over time.
claims.reasoning: Clouds reflect a large share of sunlight (NASA) and evaporation depends on absorbed surface energy (CL05); the size of the effect depends on cloud type and is not modelled.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Narrate "would slowly weaken"; label LIKELY · EXACT EFFECT UNCERTAIN.

claims.statement: Where temperatures stay below freezing, such as Antarctica and high mountains, the precipitation would fall as snow, not rain.

creative_direction.logline: One raindrop hits the driest sand on Earth, and we follow a planet of nonstop drizzle from the Sahara to the sea, a rain gauge, a wheat field and a solar farm, until the clouds starve the rain of the sunlight that drives it.
creative_direction.visual_identity: Soft, silvery documentary realism: wet sand, pewter skies, glassy water and muted greens, with warm amber only for sunlight and the final sunrise. Schematics are clean and calm.
creative_direction.lighting: Flat, even overcast for most shots; a single gap of sunlight over the sea; harsh space sunlight for orbital views; low warm sunrise for the ending.
creative_direction.camera_language: Macro raindrop to wide dunes, slow orbits from space, schematic push-downs, low glides over the sea, macro glass, low ground-level shoots, eye-level farm and solar shots, and the reverse of the opening move to close the loop.
creative_direction.motion_language: Slow, deliberate moves; rain is constant but gentle; changes read as darkening, filling, greening or thinning.
creative_direction.world_scale_policy: Earth-surface shots use metres at true scale (dunes up to about 15 m, wheat 0.9 m, person 1.75 m, glass 10.5 cm). Orbital shots use 1 unit = 1 Earth radius with NASA imagery. The air column and rain gauges are labelled schematics; drop sizes and vapour specks are enlarged for visibility and labelled.
creative_direction.opening_hook: Macro of bone-dry Saharan sand: a single raindrop lands, then rain spreads across the whole dune sea as the question is asked.
creative_direction.ending_payoff: Sunlight breaks through over the dunes, the rain stops, and the camera settles back on the dry sand of the first frame.
creative_direction.loop_connection: The final frame is the frame-0 macro of dry sand, ready for the first drop again.
creative_direction.asset_policy: Reuse the studio library first (Earth and NASA textures, starfield, sky dome, ocean surface, terrain, grass field, humanoid, glass, dial gauge, particle fall (as rising vapour), bokeh, captions, labels, camera rig, pipeline and audio kit). New rain, dune, cloud-ceiling, overcast-shell and solar-panel components are original procedural work promoted to the library.

audio.voice_style: Calm, peaceful, warm adult male; intimate documentary voice; natural breathing; wonder without shouting
audio.music_direction: Sparse original pad in D minor with soft felt-piano notes like falling drops; a warm major lift for the greening Sahara; a hollow, thinning texture for the twist; resolving to D major as the sun returns.
audio.sfx_direction: Synthesized and gentle: a single drop tap, steady soft rain hiss, drizzle ticking on glass and wood, sea ambience, rain on wheat and panel glass, liquid fill sounds for the gauges, a reversed swell for the twist. No thunder or loud impacts.

captions.style: Premium documentary subtitles: ivory semibold with a thin charcoal outline and soft shadow, restrained amber active word, phrase-by-phrase with a 120 ms ease; a soft dark band behind text over bright skies.
captions.active_word_treatment: The spoken word turns amber without moving the baseline; emphasised phrases keep a soft accent, a 1.04 scale or a gentle glow.
captions.highlights_policy: Exact narration only. In-scene labels are limited to TODAY / WHAT IF chips, schematic or illustrative tags and approximate numbers backed by the claim register.

distribution.primary_search_intent: what if it rained forever everywhere on earth
distribution.distinctive_angle: Nonstop rain everywhere would not drown the world: the sky holds only 2.5 cm of water, so rain is recycled by sunlight into a gentle 3 mm-a-day drizzle that greens the Sahara, shortchanges rainforests, soaks harvests and dims solar panels, while the clouds slowly starve the rain of sunlight.
distribution.seo_integrity_note: Figures are global averages from USGS and NASA (2.5 cm of water in the air, about a metre of rain a year from the energy budget); greening, harvest and solar effects are presented as possibilities, and the rain-weakening twist as likely with uncertain size. Titles must not promise floods or apocalypse.
